segments.voice: Episode one of a long series. A character turns to the camera and tells you everything: who leaves home, who gets taken, who wins the war, how it ends. Spoilers, all of them, in the first ten minutes. That's chapter one of the Ramayana. Narada answers Valmiki's question with the entire story, start to finish, in about a hundred verses. And people have kept reading the hundreds of chapters that follow anyway.
screen: `EPISODE ONE TELLS YOU EVERYTHING.` → `A HUNDRED VERSES, START TO FINISH.` → `AND PEOPLE KEEP READING.`

segments.voice: Here's Narada's outline. Rama, the eldest son of King Dasharatha, deeply loved, is about to be made heir. But a queen, Kaikeyi, calls in two promises the king once made her: exile for Rama, the throne for her own son Bharata. Rama goes to the forest without a word of protest, and his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana go with him. The king dies of grief. Bharata refuses the throne and rules only in Rama's name. In the forest, the demon king Ravana carries Sita off. Rama searches, befriends the monkey king Sugriva, and Hanuman leaps the ocean to find her in Lanka. A bridge is built, a war is fought, Ravana falls, and Rama comes home to rule. The whole epic, in a single chapter. It's known as the short Ramayana. Why give it all away? Remember Valmiki's question: is anyone good all the way through? The Ramayana isn't asking what happens. It's asking how to live. How a son keeps his father's word. How a brother says no to a crown that isn't his. How a wife holds firm. Hindus call that dharma: the right way to act, the order that holds a life and a world together. Many Hindus call Rama maryada purushottama, the best of people, who never steps outside dharma's bounds. So the story is built for return, not suspense. Grandparents tell it to children who already know it. At Ramlila plays each autumn, the audience knows the ending before the curtain rises. You don't come back to find out who wins. You come back to watch how Rama answers, and to ask how you would. Narada even ends with a promise: whoever reads this story of Rama is blessed by it.

492.title: The poet from the anthill
492.hook: a poet named after an anthill, and the robber turned around by Rama's name

492.howItsDone: Valmiki Jayanti, his birthday, is celebrated on the full moon of the month of Ashvin, especially by the Valmiki community, who honor him as their guru; Narada appears across Hindu scripture and is remembered as a great devotee of Vishnu.

segments.voice: Valmika is a Sanskrit word for an anthill, the tall mound of earth termites and ants build. Tradition hears the poet's name, Valmiki, as the one from the anthill. Why would anyone be named that? There's a story people tell, a story of a changed life, told across India in many languages. But here's the honest part: Valmiki's own Ramayana doesn't tell it. In his own book he is simply a hermit, living by a river, asking a good question.
screen: `VALMIKA: AN ANTHILL.` → `THE ONE FROM THE ANTHILL.` → `A STORY HIS OWN BOOK DOESN'T TELL.`

segments.voice: Start with Narada. He's a devarshi, a sage of the gods, and he turns up across Hindu storytelling. He wanders between heaven and earth, carries news, asks the question that sets things moving, and in later tradition he walks with a vina, singing the name of Vishnu. Now Valmiki. Some later texts and retellings say he began life as a highway robber, often called Ratnakara, who robbed travelers to feed his family. One day he stopped a group of sages, sometimes Narada himself. They asked: will your family share the weight of your wrongdoing? He went home and asked. They said no. Shaken, he asked the sages for help, and was given the name of Rama to repeat. He couldn't even say it properly, so he said mara, mara, which run together becomes Rama, Rama. He sat so long that an anthill rose over him, and the man who came out was Valmiki, the one from the anthill. That story is found in later works, not in Valmiki's Sanskrit text, where he is simply a muni, a quiet sage. So why do Hindus keep telling it? Because it carries a big teaching: nama japa, repeating the name of God. Many Hindu traditions hold that the name itself has power, that saying it again and again, even clumsily, turns a person toward God. That's why you'll see Hindus counting a name on a mala of a hundred and eight beads, or saying Rama, Rama under their breath. And it says something else: no one is too far gone. A robber can become the first poet. Today the Valmiki community, in North India especially, honors him as its own guru.

segments.voice: Narada has gone. Valmiki walks down to the Tamasa river to bathe, his student Bharadvaja carrying his bark cloth. The water, Valmiki says, is clear, the way a good person's mind is clear. On a branch near the bank, two birds, a pair, are calling to each other, lost in each other. Then, out of nowhere, an arrow. A hunter has shot the male. He falls, bleeding, and the female circles, crying. Valmiki watches. Something rises in his throat, and he speaks.
screen: `DOWN TO THE TAMASA RIVER.` → `TWO BIRDS ON A BRANCH.` → `AN ARROW. A CRY.`

segments.voice: What he says is a curse: ma nishada pratishtham tvam agamah shashvatih samah, yat kraunchamithunad ekam avadhih kamamohitam. Hunter, may you never find rest for endless years, because you killed one of a pair of krauncha birds, lost in love. The bird is sometimes called a crow in English, but krauncha is usually a curlew or a crane: a big, long-legged water bird. Now the surprise. Valmiki stops, troubled. Grief made him curse a man, and that bothers him. But then he notices how it came out. Four quarters, each the same number of syllables, a rhythm you could set to a lute. He'd spoken in perfect measure without trying. And he names it: this was born of shoka, grief, so let it be called shloka, verse. That's the tradition's story of the first poem. Not from ambition, not for a king's praise, but from compassion for a bird he didn't know. That's why Valmiki is called the adikavi, the first poet. Hindu tradition takes the moment seriously. The great Sanskrit critic Anandavardhana said the soul of a poem is the feeling it carries, and his example is this one: the first poet's grief for the parted birds became verse. Many read the whole Ramayana as carrying that feeling, karuna, compassion, from its first verse on. And notice whose grief it was. Not a king's. A bird's. Many Hindu teachings see the same Self in every creature, and that's one reason ahimsa, non-harm, reaches to animals. The epic of Rama begins with one man who couldn't look away from a bird's sorrow.
screen: `A CURSE, SPOKEN IN GRIEF.` · `KRAUNCHA: A CRANE OR CURLEW.` · `SHOKA, GRIEF, BECOMES SHLOKA, VERSE.` · `KARUNA: COMPASSION, FOR A BIRD.` · then, large: `MĀ NIṢĀDA PRATIṢṬHĀṂ TVAM.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: krauncha, and the hunter's arrow. Valmiki's grief, shoka, poured out as verse, shloka: the first poem, born of compassion.

segments.voice: Valmiki goes back to his hermitage, but he can't let it go. He bathes, he sits, and the verse keeps playing in his head, and he is uneasy about the curse he spoke. You know the feeling: a sentence you said today, replaying at night. Then a visitor arrives. Brahma himself, the creator, four-faced, the one the whole world comes from. And Valmiki, still lost in the bird's grief, can't stop saying the verse, even in front of him.
screen: `REPLAYING IT AT NIGHT.` → `A VISITOR: BRAHMA.` → `STILL SAYING THE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Brahma smiles and settles it. Don't be troubled, he says. That verse came from me; it was meant to. Now tell the whole story of Rama, as Narada told it to you, in this same meter. Not one word you speak in this poem will be false. Then the promise people still quote: as long as mountains stand and rivers flow on the earth, so long will the story of Rama be told. Valmiki sits on a seat of sacred grass and turns inward. The whole story comes to him in vision. The tradition gives the count: twenty-four thousand verses. Two boys live in his hermitage, twins with beautiful voices, Kusha and Lava. He teaches them the whole poem by heart, and they sing it to sages and later in a king's court. Here's the turn: the twins are Rama's own sons, though Rama doesn't know them yet. The story will be sung to its own hero. And that's why, for Hindus, the Ramayana isn't only a book to read. It's a story to say aloud and to hear, and doing that is worship. Families and temples hold readings. Many recite one book, often the Sundara Kanda, Hanuman's book, as a prayer. And before a reading, an old verse honors Valmiki as a cuckoo, sitting on the branch of poetry, singing Rama, Rama, sweetly. So if you have seen a grandmother read the Ramayana aloud, verse by verse, even the long lists, that is not slowness. It is prayer, and sitting beside her and listening counts too.

segments.voice: Sit like Valmiki on his grass seat. If you don't pray, just listen: play a minute of someone chanting the Ramayana or the Sundara Kanda, and hear it the way the sages heard the twins.

segments.voice: The first thing Valmiki gives us is a city. Ayodhya, on the river Sarayu, in the land of Kosala. Wide straight roads sprinkled with water and strewn with flowers, gates and arches, music, merchants, horses, elephants, full granaries. In his telling, nobody there is greedy, nobody lies, nobody is without learning or without food. A city working as it should. And at its center sits a king who has everything, and who can't sleep for wanting the one thing he doesn't have.

segments.voice: The king is Dasharatha, of the line of Ikshvaku. His name means ten chariots. He's wise, generous, a famous warrior, guided by great counselors like the sage Vasishtha. He has three chief queens: Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. And he has no son. For a king in the epic's world, that isn't only personal sorrow. It's the line, the ancestors' rites, the kingdom's future. So Dasharatha decides: I will perform the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice, for the sake of sons. Notice how he does it. He doesn't act alone. He lays out his grief to his priests and ministers, and asks. They approve. And his charioteer, Sumantra, remembers an old prophecy about a young sage named Rishyashringa, whose story is strange enough for tomorrow. Now the teaching under the scene. A sacrifice, a yajna, is the oldest form of Hindu worship: offerings poured into a fire with sacred words. Agni, the fire, is the messenger who carries them to the gods. The Bhagavad Gita puts it simply: nourish the gods with sacrifice, and they will nourish you. Give, and receive; a circle. Hindu families still live inside that circle. At a wedding, the couple walks around the fire. Before moving into a new home, many families hold a havan: a small fire, ghee and grain poured in, with svaha at each offering. So the Ramayana's first real scene isn't heroic at all. It's a good man admitting what he lacks, asking the people around him, and bringing his longing to the sacred fire.

segments.voice: At a havan, each offering goes into the fire with one word: svaha. Let one longing come up, something you've wanted a long time, and hold it honestly. If you pray, offer it on an out-breath, silently saying svaha, and let the fire have it. If you don't, simply name it, then name one person you could ask for help, as Dasharatha did.

496.title: The boy who brought the rain
496.hook: a forest boy welcomes strangers as guests and the rain follows him; why Hindus treat the guest as God
496.carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is God
496.tomorrow: why did Ravana never fear a human?
496.howItsDone: Rishyashringa is honored at some local temples in India, and his story is told as part of the Ramayana's opening, as the reason the rain-bringing sage leads Dasharatha's rites.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-NINETY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's sacrifice begins, and your line: yajna, bringing what you lack to the sacred fire. Sumantra remembered a prophecy.
screen: `A KING WHO ASKED FOR HELP.`

segments.voice: Deep in a forest lives a sage, Vibhandaka, and his son, Rishyashringa. The boy has grown up with only his father, the trees, the sacred fire and the animals. He has never been to a town, never seen anyone but his father. Meanwhile, in the kingdom of Anga, a long way off, the rain has stopped. Fields crack. Wells sink. The king, Romapada, asks his priests what to do, and they give him an odd answer: bring the forest boy here, and the rain will come with him.
screen: `A BOY WHO'S ONLY SEEN HIS FATHER.` → `A KINGDOM WITHOUT RAIN.` → `BRING THE FOREST BOY.`

segments.voice: Here's how Sumantra tells it. The king's people can't march in and take a sage's son. So they send young women from the city into the forest, with sweets and garlands. Rishyashringa, who has never met anyone, thinks they're young hermits from another ashram, and welcomes them the way a host should: water, a seat, roots and fruit. They give him sweets he takes for a new kind of fruit, and invite him to their hermitage. It's a gentle trick, but no one lays a hand on him. He goes with them, all the way to Anga, and the moment he enters the kingdom, the rain pours down. The king honors him and gives him his daughter, Shanta, in marriage. Dasharatha hears this, goes himself to Anga, to his old friend Romapada, and brings Rishyashringa and Shanta home to Ayodhya with great honor. Then, on the bank of the Sarayu, the horse is released to wander for a year before the great rite. Look at how everyone behaves in this story. The forest boy receives strangers as honored guests. The king of Anga invites him and gives him a family. Dasharatha travels in person to bring the sage home. It's hospitality all the way down, and Hinduism makes that a teaching: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you, a line from the Taittiriya Upanishad. That's why a Hindu grandmother won't let you leave without eating, why guests are served first, why many temples feed whoever comes. And in this story, where the guest is honored, the sky answers.

497.title: Four sons from the fire
497.hook: a demon king who scorned humans, and why God comes down as one
497.carry: avatar: God comes down as one of us
497.howItsDone: Hindus celebrate Rama Navami, Rama's birthday, on the ninth day of the bright half of Chaitra, with fasting, temple worship, readings of the Ramayana, and in some places a cradle for the infant Rama.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-NINETY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the boy who brought the rain, and your line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is God. Rishyashringa came, and a horse was set free for a year.
screen: `THE GUEST IS GOD.`

segments.voice: While the priests on earth pour offerings into Dasharatha's fire, the gods hold a meeting of their own. They go to Brahma with a complaint. Ravana, king of the rakshasas, is tormenting all the worlds, and nobody can stop him. Why not? Because Brahma himself gave him a boon. Ravana asked never to be killed by gods, or demons, or celestial beings of any kind. He listed nearly everyone, and left out one group, because he thought them too weak to bother with.
screen: `THE GODS HOLD A MEETING.` → `RAVANA'S BOON.` → `HE LEFT OUT ONE GROUP.`

segments.voice: Ravana left out human beings. He scorned them. So Brahma says: he can be killed by a human. And Vishnu agrees to be born as a man, in four parts, as the four sons of Dasharatha. Down on earth, Rishyashringa begins a second rite, for the sake of sons. Out of the fire rises a great shining being, carrying a golden vessel. Inside is payasa, sweet rice cooked in milk, made by the gods. Give this to your queens, he tells Dasharatha. The king divides it: half to Kausalya, and the rest shared between Sumitra and Kaikeyi, Sumitra receiving two shares. In time, four sons are born. Rama to Kausalya, on the ninth day of the bright half of Chaitra. Bharata to Kaikeyi. And to Sumitra, twins: Lakshmana and Shatrughna. The loophole is the whole point. Ravana thought humans didn't count, and God came as one. Hindus call this avatar, literally a descent: Vishnu coming down into the world in the form it needs. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that whenever dharma declines, he comes, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma right. So Rama Navami isn't only a birthday. Hindus keep it with fasting, readings of the Ramayana, and in some temples a cradle for the infant Rama: God, small enough to rock. Now the week, from the top. The whole story in chapter one. The poet from the anthill. Two birds, and grief becoming verse. Brahma's promise. A king at the sacred fire. A guest who brought the rain. And today, four boys, and God come down as one of us.
screen: `RAVANA SCORNED HUMAN BEINGS.` · `A VESSEL OF PAYASA FROM THE FIRE.` · `AVATAR: GOD COMES DOWN.` · `RAMA NAVAMI.` · then, large: `RAMA, BHARATA, LAKSHMANA, SHATRUGHNA.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus chant a short mantra to Rama: Shri Rama, Jaya Rama, Jaya Jaya Rama. If you pray, say it softly with the breath. If you don't, bring to mind one ordinary person, the kind Ravana would have overlooked, and breathe as if they matter. In this story, the one nobody counted is where God turned up.
Dasharatha's sacrifice. Its fruit is the payasa from the fire, shared among three queens, and four sons, born to undo Ravana's boast.
screen: `DASHARATHA'S SACRIFICE — today's word`.
